source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether MoE helps a serving workload. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Define the serving question first: compare MoE with a matched dense or alternative baseline at equal quality target, precision, hardware, software, model interface, and workload. Sweep request length mix, arrival rate/concurrency, batch policy, and prefill/decode composition. Mechanism: the router selects top-k experts, then dispatch/combine moves activations to expert owners; record router, expert, communication, and synchronization time separately. Warm up, randomize trial order, repeat enough runs for confidence intervals, and report tokens/s, requests/s, TTFT, inter-token latency, p50/p95/p99, peak memory, power if relevant, errors, drops/reroutes, and quality. Boundary: lower active FLOPs do not guarantee a serving win when routing is skewed, capacity overflows, or all-to-all links saturate; extrapolation beyond tested load is not justified.
risks: Unequal quality, quantization, batching, or admission policy can confound the comparison.
Average throughput can hide queueing, overflow, and tail-latency regressions.
evidence_required: Matched baseline, quality target, router top-k, capacity/overflow policy, topology, precision, workload and load sweep.
Repeated phase-specific timings, expert-load and drop counts, memory high-water marks, latency percentiles, throughput, errors, and quality results.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether MoE helps a serving workload. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Use a matched experiment with the MoE and comparator serving the same prompts, output-quality target, precision, hardware, runtime, and request-length/concurrency distributions. Sweep offered load and batch/concurrency policy, separate prefill from decode, warm up, randomize runs, and repeat to estimate variance. Mechanism: top-k routing dispatches activations to selected experts and combines their outputs, so instrument router time, expert compute, dispatch/combine, synchronization, and queueing. Report TTFT, inter-token latency, p50/p95/p99, throughput/goodput, peak memory, expert utilization, overflow/drops/reroutes, errors, and quality. Boundary: results from balanced synthetic traffic may not hold for skewed production prompts or a different interconnect/topology.
risks: Load shape and prompt mix can change routing balance and serving tails.
Performance gains may be accompanied by silent token drops or quality changes.
evidence_required: Exact model/baseline, quality checks, precision, topology, routing/capacity settings, workload mix, and load sweep.
Repeated phase timings, expert histograms, communication traces, overflow accounting, memory, latency tails, throughput, errors, and quality.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether MoE helps a serving workload. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Establish a quality-matched comparator and freeze model, precision, hardware, runtime, and serving configuration except for the MoE choice. Test representative prompt lengths, output lengths, arrival rates, concurrency, batch policy, and prefill/decode phases; warm up and repeat trials with confidence intervals. Mechanism: router assignments cause token scatter to expert ranks, expert execution, and gather/combine, which should be timed separately from dense compute and scheduling. Measure TTFT, inter-token latency, p50/p95/p99, throughput/goodput, peak per-device memory, expert load, communication, overflow, failures, and output quality. Boundary: an MoE result is workload- and topology-specific; capacity overflow or communication saturation can reverse benefits at higher concurrency.
risks: Changing batching or quality target invalidates simple baseline comparisons.
Per-device memory and communication bottlenecks can be hidden by aggregate averages.
evidence_required: Matched quality and workload, hardware/topology, precision, router top-k, capacity/overflow policy, and batch/admission settings.
Per-phase latency, expert loads, dispatch/combine traces, peak memory, throughput, overflow/errors, and quality with repeated trials.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether MoE helps a serving workload. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Plan a controlled A/B benchmark against a dense or other baseline matched for quality, hardware, precision, software, tokenizer, request mix, and service limits. Sweep batch size, concurrency, arrival rate, sequence lengths, and prefill/decode mix; warm up, repeat trials, and summarize uncertainty rather than a single best run. Mechanism: top-k routing dispatches tokens across experts and combines results, adding communication, synchronization, and temporary buffers; trace each component. Measure tokens/s and requests/s, TTFT, inter-token latency, p50/p95/p99, peak memory, expert imbalance, overflow/drops, errors, and quality. Boundary: active-compute savings are not a universal serving improvement when experts are imbalanced, batches are small, or bandwidth and capacity limits dominate.
risks: A benchmark can overstate gains if it omits skewed traffic or tail latency.
Overflow handling may change outputs while improving nominal throughput.
evidence_required: Matched comparator and quality, model/runtime/precision, topology, routing and capacity policy, workload and load ranges.
Repeated phase-aware metrics, router/expert/communication telemetry, memory, tail latency, throughput, failures, and quality.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about MoE? Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: State the model and quality target, dense/comparator definition, precision, hardware and topology, runtime/kernel versions, expert count and placement, router top-k and capacity/overflow policy, batching/admission policy, and workload distributions for prompt/output lengths, concurrency, and arrival rate. Mechanism: token routing selects experts, then dispatch/combine and synchronization add communication and buffering beyond expert compute. Define whether the claim concerns prefill, decode, training, throughput, latency, cost, or memory, and report units and percentiles. Boundary: active FLOPs or total parameters alone do not predict serving performance; skew, small batches, capacity overflow, and interconnect saturation can reverse the claim.
risks: An unspecified comparator or quality target makes speedup claims uninterpretable.
Routing and placement details can dominate results and vary by workload.
evidence_required: Complete configuration, workload/load distribution, matched baseline and quality evaluation.
Phase-specific latency/throughput/memory data plus expert load, overflow, communication, failures, and uncertainty.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about MoE? Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Specify the claim's metric and phase, model quality/equivalence, comparator, precision, hardware, topology, software, expert sharding/replication, router top-k, capacity factor, overflow behavior, batch/concurrency policy, and representative prompt/output length and arrival distributions. Mechanism: the router creates token-to-expert assignments; distributed dispatch and result combination introduce all-to-all traffic, synchronization, and buffers. Distinguish active expert compute from total resident memory, and define cost and units. Boundary: no general latency or throughput conclusion follows from active parameter count or FLOPs when routing is skewed, links are congested, or capacity is exceeded.
risks: Unmatched quality, precision, or batching can create false speedups.
Aggregate utilization can mask hot experts, drops, and tail latency.
evidence_required: Versioned configuration and matched quality/workload baseline, including routing, capacity, topology, and load.
Expert-level load and overflow, communication traces, memory high-water marks, latency percentiles, throughput, errors, and quality.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about MoE? Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Before claiming a benefit, state the target metric (for example requests/s, tokens/s, TTFT, p99 inter-token latency, memory, or cost), phase, quality criterion, baseline, hardware/topology, precision, runtime, and all relevant MoE settings: experts, sharding, top-k, capacity and overflow policy. Also state batch/admission policy and prompt/output length, concurrency, and arrival distributions. Mechanism: routing dispatches activations to selected expert owners and combines outputs, so communication and synchronization may dominate expert-compute savings. Boundary: results at one balanced load point cannot be generalized to skewed traffic, another phase, or a saturated topology.
risks: Metric selection can hide a regression in another user-facing dimension.
Capacity and fallback behavior can affect both quality and performance.
evidence_required: Explicit metric definitions, matched quality/baseline, complete system and workload assumptions.
Phase-aware repeated measurements with expert-load, overflow, communication, memory, latency, throughput, failure, and quality data.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about MoE? Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Document model quality and comparator, metric definitions and units, prefill/decode or other phase, hardware/topology, precision, implementation versions, expert placement, router top-k, capacity factor, overflow/fallback/drop policy, batching, and workload/load distribution. Mechanism: selected-token assignments require scatter/dispatch, expert execution, and gather/combine; these add communication, synchronization, and memory buffering. Separate active compute, total resident weights, activation/KV memory, and measured device high-water marks. Boundary: MoE is not inherently faster or smaller; skewed routing, long requests, low concurrency, capacity overflow, or limited bandwidth can eliminate or reverse a claimed gain.
risks: Comparisons based only on theoretical FLOPs or parameter counts may mislead.
Different sharding or replication changes memory and communication without changing the abstract model.
evidence_required: Versioned model/system settings, matched quality comparator, representative workload and load range.
Expert routing/overflow, communication, per-device memory, phase latency, throughput, errors, and repeated quality measurements.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about MoE? Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: State what is held constant: model quality, comparator, hardware, topology, precision, runtime, tokenizer, and serving policy. Specify experts, sharding/replication, top-k routing, capacity and overflow handling, batch/concurrency/admission, workload lengths and arrival mix, and whether the claim concerns prefill, decode, throughput, latency, memory, or cost. Mechanism: router assignments trigger activation dispatch to expert owners and output combine, with communication and synchronization that can offset reduced expert compute. Boundary: a result is only supported over the tested workload and load range; hot experts, small batches, saturated links, or resident expert-weight memory can negate the apparent benefit.
risks: Changing quality or service policy can confound the claimed effect.
Averages and theoretical active FLOPs can conceal capacity, memory, and p99 regressions.
evidence_required: Matched baseline/quality and full model, runtime, topology, precision, routing, capacity, and workload assumptions.
Repeated phase-specific latency/throughput/memory measurements, expert load, communication, overflow, failures, and quality.

source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: During training, each token is routed to selected experts in a teacher-forced forward pass and the router/expert weights receive gradient updates; activation memory, backward communication, optimizer state, and microbatch scheduling matter. During inference, weights are fixed and serving routes prompt tokens during prefill and one or a few new tokens per decode step, often with KV-cache reuse; dispatch/combine, batching, queueing, and latency tails dominate. Mechanism: top-k assignments require capacity-constrained dispatch to expert owners and output combination in both phases. Boundary: training throughput or active-FLOP results do not predict inference latency—decode has smaller, dynamic batches and different memory/communication pressure, and overflow or routing skew may change quality.
risks: Training and inference use different phases, batching, gradients, and memory lifetimes.
KV-cache and serving traffic can make decode behavior unlike training or prefill.
evidence_required: Phase, sequence lengths, batch/concurrency, routing/capacity policy, topology, precision, and cache settings.
Separate forward/backward versus prefill/decode timings, expert loads, communication, memory, latency/throughput, overflow, failures, and quality.
